screens.title: Understanding Layouts and View Groups
screens.narratorSegment: In this chapter we'll build a clear mental model of Android's UI: the small, interactive units called Views and the container objects called ViewGroups that arrange them. You will learn the practical differences between common containers, how simple XML attributes control size and position, and how to avoid the most common layout pitfalls. This matters because every app screen you make is built from these pieces. For example, placing three buttons that share available space correctly depends on choosing the right ViewGroup and using layout_weight. We'll show concrete XML you can paste into a layout file, then explain why dp and sp exist and how they keep interfaces consistent across devices. You will also compare LinearLayout and RelativeLayout patterns so you can pick the simpler, more efficient structure for a given design. By the end of this chapter you'll be able to choose whether to stack elements, position by relation, or rethink a deeply nested hierarchy that slows rendering. Think of this as learning the room and furniture of your UI before arranging a complete screen.

screens.title: What is a View and what is a ViewGroup?
screens.narratorSegment: Let's define the two fundamental terms you will use on every Android screen. A View is a single rectangular element that draws content and handles user input. Examples include TextView, Button and ImageView. A View encapsulates drawing logic and input callbacks; it does one visual job. A ViewGroup is itself a View but adds the ability to contain other Views and manage their layout rules. Think of a View as a piece of furniture and a ViewGroup as a room that arranges furniture according to rules. For a concrete example: a TextView shows a string and reacts to clicks, while a LinearLayout stacks several TextViews vertically. A common misconception is to treat ViewGroups only as wrappers; in fact they are layout managers: they measure children, decide sizes, and position them. That measurement step can be costly if your tree is deep. When you design screens, ask: am I placing content or arranging content? If the element only renders content, it's a View. If it arranges children, it's a ViewGroup. A quick takeaway: minimizing unnecessary ViewGroups simplifies measurement and improves performance. What part of a screen you can replace with a single View rather than a container?

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: View = draws and handles input. ViewGroup = contains and arranges Views. Treat groups as layout managers, not mere wrappers.

content.html:
Core Concept

View vs ViewGroup

A concise definitional comparison and practical examples to anchor the distinction.

View — single drawable element
  • Draws its own content and processes input events.
  • Examples: TextView, Button, ImageView.
ViewGroup — container and manager
  • Holds and arranges child views and runs measure/layout passes.
  • Examples: LinearLayout, RelativeLayout, ConstraintLayout.
Concrete example
A Button is a View that draws text and responds to clicks. A LinearLayout is a ViewGroup that stacks that Button with other Views.
Key Takeaway

Design screens by asking whether an element draws content or arranges other elements; minimize unnecessary containers.

Analogy

Room and furniture

Treat a ViewGroup as the room and Views as furniture. Rooms arrange furniture; furniture performs a function.

Misconception
Wrapping every element in multiple ViewGroups won't change appearance but will slow measurement and layout passes. Use a single appropriate container when possible.
Check your understanding
Look at a sample screen: can you remove one container without changing layout? If yes, simplify it.

screens.title: LinearLayout fundamentals
screens.narratorSegment: LinearLayout arranges its child views in a single row or column. The direction is controlled by the android:orientation attribute set to either horizontal or vertical. This simple rule makes LinearLayout ideal for lists of related items, toolbars, or stacked form fields. A practical pattern is to set a child's dimension to zero in the stacking direction and then give it a layout_weight; the parent will distribute the remaining space proportionally. For example, in a horizontal LinearLayout three buttons with layout_width set to zero and layout_weight of one each will share the available width equally. A common pitfall is to mix wrap_content with weight incorrectly — when using weights, set the measured dimension to 0dp so the weight system can take control. Another point: layout_gravity positions a child within extra space inside its cell; gravity controls content inside the child. Concrete example: build a horizontal row of three equal buttons using android:layout_width="0dp" and android:layout_weight="1" for each. Misconception check: weights are not a replacement for flexible constraints in complex UIs; they are a simple tool for proportional distribution. Try converting a nested set of layouts into a single LinearLayout with weights where appropriate.

keyIdea.title: LinearLayout rule
keyIdea.text: Use android:orientation to stack children and layout_weight with 0dp to share space proportionally.

content.html:
Definition

LinearLayout fundamentals

Understand orientation, weight, and best practices for proportional layouts.

Orientation
Set android:orientation to vertical or horizontal to control stacking direction.
Weight system
Give children android:layout_width or height of 0dp in the stacking axis and assign android:layout_weight to share available space.
Concrete example
Three equal buttons: set each button's width to 0dp and weight to 1 inside a horizontal LinearLayout.
Key Takeaway

Weights provide simple proportional sizing. Use 0dp along the weight axis so the layout system can allocate space predictably.

Process
  1. Choose orientation: horizontal for rows, vertical for stacks.
  2. Decide which children need proportional space.
  3. Set stacking-axis size to 0dp for those children.
  4. Assign layout_weight values to control proportions.
  5. Use layout_gravity for child alignment inside available cell space.
Common mistake
Using wrap_content for weighted children prevents weights from taking effect. Always set the axis dimension to 0dp when using weight.

screens.title: Key XML attributes: match_parent, wrap_content, dp, and sp
screens.narratorSegment: A small set of XML attributes determine most layout behavior. android:layout_width and android:layout_height accept match_parent to expand to the parent's available space, and wrap_content to size to the content. Choosing between them determines whether a view occupies the whole line or only what it needs. Units matter: dp is density-independent pixels and is the correct unit for layout dimensions and margins because it keeps physical sizes consistent across screens. For text, use sp — scale-independent pixels — because sp respects the user’s font size preference in accessibility settings. A common beginner mistake is to use px which ties the UI to raw pixels leading to inconsistent sizes on different devices. Another important attribute is android:layout_gravity which positions a child inside extra parent space, distinct from gravity which controls content inside a view. Concrete example: to make a button stretch across the width set layout_width="match_parent" and to make text readable on different devices set textSize="18sp" rather than using px. Remember: pick match_parent when you need full coverage, wrap_content when the view should shrink to its content, dp for layouts, and sp for text.

keyIdea.title: Sizing essentials
keyIdea.text: Use match_parent or wrap_content for sizing; use dp for dimensions and sp for text to keep interfaces consistent and accessible.

content.html:
Definition

match_parent vs wrap_content

These values tell a view how much space to claim from its parent in a dimension.

match_parent
Expand to fill the parent's remaining space in that dimension.
wrap_content
Size to fit the view's own content only.
Units: dp vs sp
Use dp for layout sizes and margins; use sp for text sizes so the UI respects user font preferences.
Concrete Example
<Button
    android:layout_width="match_parent"
    android:layout_height="wrap_content"
    android:text="Click Me"
    android:textSize="18sp" />
Misconception
Using px for text or layout ties your design to raw pixels and breaks consistency across devices. Prefer dp and sp.

screens.title: Using layout_weight to distribute space
screens.narratorSegment: Here we'll walk through an XML example that uses layout_weight to distribute space across children. The key idea is to let the LinearLayout measure remaining space and divide it according to weight values. Start with a horizontal LinearLayout, set each button's layout_width to 0dp, and assign android:layout_weight="1" to each. This tells the system to measure content independently, then allocate the parent’s available width proportionally. A concrete snippet shows this in action and can be pasted into activity_main. xml. A common misconception is to think weights work when children have wrap_content widths; they do not. If you leave width as wrap_content, weight won't control the final size as intended. Another subtlety: weights sum up, so different weight numbers create different shares. For example, weights of 1, 2, and 1 produce a center button twice as wide as the others. After writing the XML, preview in the layout editor and resize the screen to see the proportional behavior. This helps you predict visual results across screen sizes before running the app. Using layout_weight to distribute space means set the stacking-axis dimension to 0dp and use layout_weight to let the parent allocate space proportionally.. In practical terms, a code walkthrough for equal-width buttons. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Code Walkthrough

Three equal buttons with layout_weight

Copy this into activity_main.xml inside a layout root to experiment.

<LinearLayout
    xmlns:android="http://schemas.android.com/apk/res/android"
    android:layout_width="match_parent"
    android:layout_height="wrap_content"
    android:orientation="horizontal">

    <Button
        android:layout_width="0dp"
        android:layout_height="wrap_content"
        android:layout_weight="1"
        android:text="One" />

    <Button
        android:layout_width="0dp"
        android:layout_height="wrap_content"
        android:layout_weight="1"
        android:text="Two" />

    <Button
        android:layout_width="0dp"
        android:layout_height="wrap_content"
        android:layout_weight="1"
        android:text="Three" />

</LinearLayout>
Misconception
Weights don't shrink content. If child content is larger than the allocated space, it still affects layout; design for realistic text lengths.
Example scenario
Use weights when you need proportional sizing across a row, such as toolbar segments, segmented controls, or evenly spaced buttons.
Key Takeaway

Use 0dp for the weighted axis and set layout_weight values; preview to ensure content fits at the smallest width you support.

screens.title: RelativeLayout basics
screens.narratorSegment: RelativeLayout positions child views by rules relative to the parent container or to other child views. You can align a view to the parent's top, bottom, start or end, center it horizontally or vertically, or place it below, above, toStartOf, or toEndOf another view by referencing that view's id. This makes RelativeLayout powerful for non-linear arrangements where elements are positioned by relationships rather than a single flow. For example, you can center a title horizontally at the top of the screen and place a button below it by setting the button's layout_below attribute to the title's id. A concrete pitfall is forgetting to give the referenced view an id before referencing it; that causes the layout to fail. Another complexity is that deep chains of relative dependencies can be hard to reason about and maintain. When you use RelativeLayout, define ids clearly and keep the rules simple. RelativeLayout is best when positions are defined by relationships; for simple stacking use LinearLayout. Ask yourself which rule expresses the design most directly: a relational rule tends to be clearer in RelativeLayout. RelativeLayout basics means relativelayout uses relationship attributes and ids to place views relative to parent or sibling views; keep dependencies simple and use ids correctly.. In practical terms, positioning views relative to parent and siblings. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Relative positioning
keyIdea.text: RelativeLayout uses relationship attributes and ids to place views relative to parent or sibling views; keep dependencies simple and use ids correctly.

content.html:
Definition

RelativeLayout basics

Position children by referencing parent edges or other child ids for flexible relational layouts.

Common attributes
  • android:layout_below="@id/other_view"
  • android:layout_centerHorizontal="true"
  • android:layout_alignParentTop="true"
Concrete example
<TextView
    android:id="@+id/titleTextView"
    android:layout_width="wrap_content"
    android:layout_height="wrap_content"
    android:text="Welcome!"
    android:layout_centerHorizontal="true"
    android:layout_alignParentTop="true" />

<Button
    android:id="@+id/startButton"
    android:layout_width="wrap_content"
    android:layout_height="wrap_content"
    android:text="Start App"
    android:layout_below="@id/titleTextView"
    android:layout_centerHorizontal="true" />
Misconception
Don't use RelativeLayout to force layouts better expressed by stacking or by modern constraint systems. Keep relations explicit and minimal.
Pro tip
Assign ids before referencing them and group rules so the layout remains readable. If you find long chains of references, consider refactoring.
Key Takeaway

RelativeLayout expresses spatial relationships. Use it when position depends on other views, and avoid complex chains that are hard to maintain.

screens.title: LinearLayout vs RelativeLayout
screens.narratorSegment: Choosing between LinearLayout and RelativeLayout comes down to the arrangement you need. LinearLayout is straightforward: use it when items stack in a single direction and when proportional space distribution via layout_weight is helpful. It's easy to reason about and great for toolbars, vertical forms, and rows of buttons. RelativeLayout is the better choice when a view's position depends on the location of another view or the parent, such as centering a title and placing a button below it. A practical example: a login form with stacked inputs is a job for LinearLayout; a header centered with a floating badge aligned to the parent corner suits RelativeLayout. A frequent misconception is that RelativeLayout is always more powerful and therefore better — but it can increase cognitive complexity and lead to long chains of rules. Another subtle point is performance: deep nested LinearLayouts combined can be slower than a flatter RelativeLayout for certain layouts, but deeply chaining references in RelativeLayout also has costs. The rule of thumb: pick the simplest layout that expresses the design clearly, test in the layout preview, and refactor if you find unnecessary nesting or excessive relational chains. Which arrangement communicates your design most directly?

content.html:
Comparison

LinearLayout vs RelativeLayout

LinearLayout
Simple stacking, weight-based proportional sizing, easy to reason about for linear flows.
RelativeLayout
Place elements relative to parent or siblings using ids for more flexible spatial relationships.
When to choose which
  • Use LinearLayout for stacked forms, rows of buttons, simple toolbars.
  • Use RelativeLayout when placement depends on sibling or parent alignment not expressible by stacking.
Example scenarios
Login screen inputs: LinearLayout. Title centered with a floating image at top-right: RelativeLayout.
Key Takeaway

Prefer the simpler layout that directly expresses the relationship you need. Refactor if you spot unnecessary complexity.

screens.title: Common pitfalls and performance
screens.narratorSegment: One regular source of bugs and poor performance is deep or unnecessary view nesting. Each ViewGroup must measure and layout its children in separate passes. When you have many nested containers, Android performs many measurements which can slow rendering and hurt frame rates, especially on lower-end devices. A common beginner pattern is nesting multiple LinearLayouts to achieve spacing and alignment that could be expressed with a single ViewGroup or with layout_weight. For example, a horizontal LinearLayout inside a vertical LinearLayout inside another horizontal LinearLayout multiplies layout passes. The practical remedy is to flatten the hierarchy: combine compatible stacks into one LinearLayout with weights, or prefer a relational container that can position multiple children without extra wrappers. Another pitfall is missing ids in RelativeLayout; referencing a non-existent id breaks positioning. Also watch heavy layouts with large images sized at full resolution — scale them to appropriate dp sizes. To profile layout costs, use the layout inspector in Android Studio; look for deeply nested branches and excessive measure calls. The takeaway: design with the minimum number of ViewGroups necessary and check behavior in previews so you avoid runtime surprises.

Another pitfall is missing ids in RelativeLayout; referencing a non-existent id breaks positioning. The takeaway: design with the minimum number of ViewGroups necessary and check behavior in previews so you avoid runtime surprises.

content.html:
Core Concept

Nesting and layout cost

Each container increases measurement and layout passes. Deep nesting multiplies cost and can slow UI rendering.

Why it matters
More measure/layout work equals longer frame times. On animations or complex screens this leads to jank.
Refactor strategies
  • Combine stacks into a single LinearLayout with weights when possible.
  • Use RelativeLayout for simple positional relationships that eliminate wrappers.
Debugging tip
Use Android Studio's Layout Inspector to spot deep branches and expensive measure calls, then simplify the hierarchy.
Example
A UI built with three nested LinearLayouts can often be re-expressed with a single LinearLayout with appropriate weights and gravity adjustments, reducing the number of measure passes.
Key Takeaway

Aim for the flattest hierarchy that expresses layout intent clearly. Measure in the preview and refactor deep nests.

screens.title: How Android renders across screen sizes
screens.narratorSegment: Android runs on a wide range of devices with different screen sizes and pixel densities. The layout system uses density-independent units to help: dp for sizes and sp for text. When you set a width in dp, Android converts that into device pixels based on the screen density, so a 100dp image occupies roughly the same physical size on different phones. Similarly, sp scales with both density and the user's preferred font size. For reliable results, test your layout in the layout editor with various device previews and orientations. The layout pass measures views using the parent constraints to compute sizes, then lays them out accordingly. If you rely on hard-coded pixel values or forget to use match_parent/wrap_content smartly, your UI will not adapt. A concrete check is to resize the preview or toggle large text accessibility to ensure text remains legible and elements do not overlap. Misconception: dpi and dp are interchangeable terms — use dp in XML for layout dimensions and sp for text. Visual testing and iterative tweaking make layouts robust across screens. fullNarratorScript:
In this chapter we'll build a clear mental model of Android's UI: the small, interactive units called Views and the container objects called ViewGroups that arrange them. You will learn the practical differences between common containers, how simple XML attributes control size and position, and how to avoid the most common layout pitfalls. This matters because every app screen you make is built from these pieces. For example, placing three buttons that share available space correctly depends on choosing the right ViewGroup and using layout_weight. We'll show concrete XML you can paste into a layout file, then explain why dp and sp exist and how they keep interfaces consistent across devices. You will also compare LinearLayout and RelativeLayout patterns so you can pick the simpler, more efficient structure for a given design. By the end of this chapter you'll be able to choose whether to stack elements, position by relation, or rethink a deeply nested hierarchy that slows rendering. Think of this as learning the room and furniture of your UI before arranging a complete screen.

By the end of this chapter you will be able to distinguish the difference between a View and a ViewGroup, pick the appropriate container for common layout problems, and apply essential XML attributes for sizing and spacing. You will practice using LinearLayout's orientation and layout_weight to build flexible rows of content, and learn how RelativeLayout positions elements using relationships and ids. The objectives also include recognizing common mistakes, such as deep nesting that increases layout passes, and using proper units: dp for layout distances and sp for text sizes so your UI respects density and user font preferences. Each objective is practical: you'll open an XML layout, apply these attributes, and preview how changes affect rendering across sizes. As you work through the hands-on profile card activity, you'll combine these skills to produce a simple and responsive layout. These objectives focus on skills you will use in nearly every Android screen you create, so mastering them reduces bugs and improves app responsiveness.

These extended objectives focus on practice and assessment readiness. You'll design a simple profile card using a vertical LinearLayout, place an ImageView, and add two TextViews for name and bio, learning how margins, padding, and gravity control spacing. You'll try setting a fixed size in dp for images and using sp for text so your app appears consistent and accessible. You'll also apply layout_weight to create equal-width buttons in a horizontal row. The assessment items ask you to choose the right layout and attributes for specific scenarios, such as equal distribution or relative positioning. Testing your changes in the layout preview will show how attributes behave on different screen sizes. Importantly, you'll practice identifying when RelativeLayout is the right tool for placing a view relative to another, and when LinearLayout's simplicity and weight system are a better fit. This prepares you to choose the most maintainable, efficient approach in real projects.

Let's define the two fundamental terms you will use on every Android screen. A View is a single rectangular element that draws content and handles user input. Examples include TextView, Button and ImageView. A View encapsulates drawing logic and input callbacks; it does one visual job. A ViewGroup is itself a View but adds the ability to contain other Views and manage their layout rules. Think of a View as a piece of furniture and a ViewGroup as a room that arranges furniture according to rules. For a concrete example: a TextView shows a string and reacts to clicks, while a LinearLayout stacks several TextViews vertically. A common misconception is to treat ViewGroups only as wrappers; in fact they are layout managers: they measure children, decide sizes, and position them. That measurement step can be costly if your tree is deep. When you design screens, ask: am I placing content or arranging content? If the element only renders content, it's a View. If it arranges children, it's a ViewGroup. A quick takeaway: minimizing unnecessary ViewGroups simplifies measurement and improves performance. What part of a screen you can replace with a single View rather than a container?

LinearLayout arranges its child views in a single row or column. The direction is controlled by the android:orientation attribute set to either horizontal or vertical. This simple rule makes LinearLayout ideal for lists of related items, toolbars, or stacked form fields. A practical pattern is to set a child's dimension to zero in the stacking direction and then give it a layout_weight; the parent will distribute the remaining space proportionally. For example, in a horizontal LinearLayout three buttons with layout_width set to zero and layout_weight of one each will share the available width equally. A common pitfall is to mix wrap_content with weight incorrectly — when using weights, set the measured dimension to 0dp so the weight system can take control. Another point: layout_gravity positions a child within extra space inside its cell; gravity controls content inside the child. Concrete example: build a horizontal row of three equal buttons using android:layout_width="0dp" and android:layout_weight="1" for each. Misconception check: weights are not a replacement for flexible constraints in complex UIs; they are a simple tool for proportional distribution. Try converting a nested set of layouts into a single LinearLayout with weights where appropriate.

A small set of XML attributes determine most layout behavior. android:layout_width and android:layout_height accept match_parent to expand to the parent's available space, and wrap_content to size to the content. Choosing between them determines whether a view occupies the whole line or only what it needs. Units matter: dp is density-independent pixels and is the correct unit for layout dimensions and margins because it keeps physical sizes consistent across screens. For text, use sp — scale-independent pixels — because sp respects the user’s font size preference in accessibility settings. A common beginner mistake is to use px which ties the UI to raw pixels leading to inconsistent sizes on different devices. Another important attribute is android:layout_gravity which positions a child inside extra parent space, distinct from gravity which controls content inside a view. Concrete example: to make a button stretch across the width set layout_width="match_parent" and to make text readable on different devices set textSize="18sp" rather than using px. Remember: pick match_parent when you need full coverage, wrap_content when the view should shrink to its content, dp for layouts, and sp for text.

Here we'll walk through an XML example that uses layout_weight to distribute space across children. The key idea is to let the LinearLayout measure remaining space and divide it according to weight values. Start with a horizontal LinearLayout, set each button's layout_width to 0dp, and assign android:layout_weight="1" to each. This tells the system to measure content independently, then allocate the parent’s available width proportionally. A concrete snippet shows this in action and can be pasted into activity_main. xml. A common misconception is to think weights work when children have wrap_content widths; they do not. If you leave width as wrap_content, weight won't control the final size as intended. Another subtlety: weights sum up, so different weight numbers create different shares. For example, weights of 1, 2, and 1 produce a center button twice as wide as the others. After writing the XML, preview in the layout editor and resize the screen to see the proportional behavior. This helps you predict visual results across screen sizes before running the app. Using layout_weight to distribute space means set the stacking-axis dimension to 0dp and use layout_weight to let the parent allocate space proportionally.. In practical terms, a code walkthrough for equal-width buttons. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

RelativeLayout positions child views by rules relative to the parent container or to other child views. You can align a view to the parent's top, bottom, start or end, center it horizontally or vertically, or place it below, above, toStartOf, or toEndOf another view by referencing that view's id. This makes RelativeLayout powerful for non-linear arrangements where elements are positioned by relationships rather than a single flow. For example, you can center a title horizontally at the top of the screen and place a button below it by setting the button's layout_below attribute to the title's id. A concrete pitfall is forgetting to give the referenced view an id before referencing it; that causes the layout to fail. Another complexity is that deep chains of relative dependencies can be hard to reason about and maintain. When you use RelativeLayout, define ids clearly and keep the rules simple. RelativeLayout is best when positions are defined by relationships; for simple stacking use LinearLayout. Ask yourself which rule expresses the design most directly: a relational rule tends to be clearer in RelativeLayout. RelativeLayout basics means relativelayout uses relationship attributes and ids to place views relative to parent or sibling views; keep dependencies simple and use ids correctly.. In practical terms, positioning views relative to parent and siblings. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Choosing between LinearLayout and RelativeLayout comes down to the arrangement you need. LinearLayout is straightforward: use it when items stack in a single direction and when proportional space distribution via layout_weight is helpful. It's easy to reason about and great for toolbars, vertical forms, and rows of buttons. RelativeLayout is the better choice when a view's position depends on the location of another view or the parent, such as centering a title and placing a button below it. A practical example: a login form with stacked inputs is a job for LinearLayout; a header centered with a floating badge aligned to the parent corner suits RelativeLayout. A frequent misconception is that RelativeLayout is always more powerful and therefore better — but it can increase cognitive complexity and lead to long chains of rules. Another subtle point is performance: deep nested LinearLayouts combined can be slower than a flatter RelativeLayout for certain layouts, but deeply chaining references in RelativeLayout also has costs. The rule of thumb: pick the simplest layout that expresses the design clearly, test in the layout preview, and refactor if you find unnecessary nesting or excessive relational chains. Which arrangement communicates your design most directly?

One regular source of bugs and poor performance is deep or unnecessary view nesting. Each ViewGroup must measure and layout its children in separate passes. When you have many nested containers, Android performs many measurements which can slow rendering and hurt frame rates, especially on lower-end devices. A common beginner pattern is nesting multiple LinearLayouts to achieve spacing and alignment that could be expressed with a single ViewGroup or with layout_weight.
